content:
# Deuteronomy Chapter 24 — Disagreement Log

**Chapter:** Deuteronomy 24 (22 verses per MT) | **Arbiter:** SOPHIA | **In council with:** EMET, LOGOS, PNEUMA

---

## v.1 — "sefer keritut": rendering of the divorce document

| Agent | Rendering |
|-------|-----------|
| EMET | "a scroll of cutting off [sefer keritut]" |
| LOGOS | "a certificate of divorce" |
| PNEUMA | "a certificate of divorce" |

**Ruling:** Hebrew *sefer keritut* = "document of cutting/severance." EMET renders literally, exposing the root metaphor of legal severance (*karat* = "to cut off"). LOGOS/PNEUMA use "certificate of divorce," the established formal rendering. The literal rendering carries exegetical value but "certificate of divorce" is the standard convention recognized throughout the tradition. Consensus follows LOGOS/PNEUMA: "certificate of divorce."

---

## v.1 — "ervat davar": rendering of the divorce grounds

| Agent | Rendering |
|-------|-----------|
| EMET | "an indecent thing [ervat davar]" |
| LOGOS | "some indecency" |
| PNEUMA | "something objectionable" |

**Ruling:** Hebrew *ervat davar* = "a matter/thing of nakedness/indecency." All three preserve the interpretive ambiguity that generated the Shammai-Hillel dispute, but via different choices. EMET brackets the Hebrew; LOGOS uses "some indecency"; PNEUMA uses "something objectionable," which drifts toward the Hillelite broad reading. Consensus follows LOGOS: "some indecency" — preserves the ambiguity without over-specifying the nature of the offense.

---

## v.1 — "she finds no favor" vs. "she becomes displeasing"

| Agent | Rendering |
|-------|-----------|
| EMET | "she finds no favor in his eyes" |
| LOGOS | "she finds no favor in his eyes" |
| PNEUMA | "she becomes displeasing to him" |

**Ruling:** Hebrew *lo timtsa' chen be-eynayw* = "she does not find favor in his eyes." EMET/LOGOS render the formula literally. PNEUMA: "she becomes displeasing to him" reverses the subject-object relationship and loses the Hebrew idiom of "finding favor." Consensus follows EMET/LOGOS.

---

## v.1–4 — Structural handling: single conditional sentence vs. broken clauses

| Agent | Rendering |
|-------|-----------|
| EMET | Preserves as a single conditional (v.1 "When a man..."; v.4 delivers the apodosis) |
| LOGOS | Preserves the conditional structure across vv.1–4 as a single extended sentence |
| PNEUMA | Breaks the unit into independent sentences; turns v.1 into a standalone description of the action |

**Ruling:** MT vv.1–4 form a single protasis-apodosis unit: the legal ruling (v.4) depends on the entire conditional setup (vv.1–3). PNEUMA's breaking of the conditional into discrete sentences obscures this grammatical and legal structure. EMET/LOGOS preserve it. Consensus follows EMET/LOGOS.

---

## v.4 — "made impure" (EMET) vs. "defiled" (LOGOS) vs. "defiled in this way" (PNEUMA)

| Agent | Rendering |
|-------|-----------|
| EMET | "after she has been made impure" |
| LOGOS | "after she has been defiled" |
| PNEUMA | "after she has become defiled in this way" |

**Ruling:** Hebrew *hutamma'ah* = Hothpa'al/Pual of *tame'* — "she has been made unclean/defiled." EMET: "made impure." LOGOS: "defiled." PNEUMA: "defiled in this way" (the addition "in this way" is interpretive). Consensus follows LOGOS: "defiled" is the established rendering of *tame'* throughout the Pentateuch.

---

## v.4 — "abomination" (EMET/LOGOS) vs. "detestable" (PNEUMA)

| Agent | Rendering |
|-------|-----------|
| EMET | "that is an abomination before the LORD" |
| LOGOS | "that is an abomination before the LORD" |
| PNEUMA | "That would be detestable to the LORD" |

**Ruling:** Hebrew *to'evah* = "abomination/detestable thing." The project has consistently rendered *to'evah* as "abomination" (cf. Leviticus chapters). PNEUMA: "detestable" is a valid but weakened equivalent. Consensus follows EMET/LOGOS: "abomination."

---

## v.5 — "newly married" subject: man vs. couple

| Agent | Rendering |
|-------|-----------|
| EMET | "When a man is newly taken as a husband" |
| LOGOS | "When a man is newly married" |
| PNEUMA | "When a man is newly married" |

**Ruling:** Hebrew *ki yiqqach ish ishah chadashah* = "when a man takes a new wife." EMET renders "newly taken as a husband" to anchor the newness to his status. LOGOS/PNEUMA: "newly married" is the natural idiomatic form. Consensus follows LOGOS/PNEUMA: "newly married."

---

## v.5 — "gladden" (EMET) vs. "bring happiness to" (LOGOS/PNEUMA)

| Agent | Rendering |
|-------|-----------|
| EMET | "shall gladden his wife whom he has taken" |
| LOGOS | "to bring happiness to his wife whom he has married" |
| PNEUMA | "bring happiness to the wife he has married" |

**Ruling:** Hebrew *vesimach et-ishto* = Piel of *simach* — "he shall make his wife rejoice/glad." EMET: "gladden." LOGOS/PNEUMA: "bring happiness to." Both are accurate; "bring happiness to" is more idiomatic in modern English. Consensus follows LOGOS/PNEUMA.

---

## v.6 — "mill or an upper millstone" vs. "pair of millstones — or even just the upper millstone"

| Agent | Rendering |
|-------|-----------|
| EMET | "No one shall take a mill or an upper millstone as a pledge" |
| LOGOS | "No one shall take a mill or an upper millstone in pledge" |
| PNEUMA | "Do not take a pair of millstones — or even just the upper millstone — as security for a debt" |

**Ruling:** Hebrew *rechayim o-rekev* = "a hand-mill or an upper millstone." EMET/LOGOS are closely aligned. PNEUMA adds "a pair of" and "or even just" (both interpretive expansions not in MT), and uses "security for a debt" for the pledge relationship. Consensus follows LOGOS: "a mill or an upper millstone in pledge."

---

## v.6 — "taking a life as a pledge" (EMET) vs. "taking a life in pledge" (LOGOS) vs. "taking a person's livelihood as security" (PNEUMA)

| Agent | Rendering |
|-------|-----------|
| EMET | "for he would be taking a life as a pledge" |
| LOGOS | "for that would be taking a life in pledge" |
| PNEUMA | "for that would be taking a person's livelihood as security" |

**Ruling:** Hebrew *ki nefesh hu' choveil* = "for it is a soul/life that he pledges." EMET/LOGOS render "life" for *nefesh*. PNEUMA renders "livelihood," interpreting the metaphor rather than translating it. "Life" (EMET/LOGOS) preserves the Hebrew force — the connection between the millstone, bread, and bare survival. Consensus follows LOGOS.

---

## v.7 — "stealing a person [nefesh]" (EMET) vs. "stealing one of his brothers" (LOGOS) vs. "kidnapping a fellow Israelite" (PNEUMA)

| Agent | Rendering |
|-------|-----------|
| EMET | "If a man is found stealing a person [nefesh] from his brothers" |
| LOGOS | "If a man is found stealing one of his brothers of the sons of Israel" |
| PNEUMA | "If someone is caught kidnapping a fellow Israelite" |

**Ruling:** Hebrew *gonev nefesh mi-echav mi-benei Yisra'el* = "stealing a soul/person from his brothers, from the sons of Israel." EMET renders *nefesh* with bracket. LOGOS restructures the Hebrew phrase. PNEUMA uses "kidnapping" (interpretive equivalent of *ganav nefesh*) and "fellow Israelite" (for "brothers from the sons of Israel"). While "kidnapping" conveys the meaning, *ganav* literally means "stealing" and that force deserves preservation. Consensus follows EMET: "stealing a person from his brothers, from the sons of Israel."

---

## v.7 — "treats him as a slave" (EMET/PNEUMA) vs. "treating him as a slave" (LOGOS)

| Agent | Rendering |
|-------|-----------|
| EMET | "he treats him as a slave and sells him" |
| LOGOS | "treating him as a slave or selling him" |
| PNEUMA | "treating him as a slave or selling him" |

**Ruling:** Hebrew *ve-hithamer bo u-makero* = "and exploited/enslaved him and sold him." The difference is the conjunction: EMET: "and sells him." LOGOS/PNEUMA: "or selling him." MT *vav* is conjunctive ("and"), not disjunctive ("or"). Consensus follows EMET: "and sells him."

---

## v.8 — "skin disease [nega tsara'at]" (EMET) vs. "leprous disease" (LOGOS) vs. "serious skin disease" (PNEUMA)

| Agent | Rendering |
|-------|-----------|
| EMET | "the skin disease [nega tsara'at]" |
| LOGOS | "leprous disease" |
| PNEUMA | "serious skin disease" |

**Ruling:** Hebrew *nega' hatsara'at* = "plague/affliction of skin disease." Project convention from Leviticus preserves *tsara'at* untranslated. EMET follows this with "skin disease [nega tsara'at]." LOGOS uses "leprous disease" (conventional formal rendering). PNEUMA: "serious skin disease" (interpretive). Leviticus convention established *tsara'at* as preserved; Deuteronomy should maintain this consistency. Consensus follows EMET: "the skin disease [nega tsara'at]."

---

## v.10 — "loan" (EMET) vs. "loan of any sort" (LOGOS) vs. "loan of any kind" (PNEUMA)

| Agent | Rendering |
|-------|-----------|
| EMET | "any [kind of] loan" |
| LOGOS | "a loan of any sort" |
| PNEUMA | "a loan of any kind" |

**Ruling:** Hebrew *mashsha't me'umah* = "a loan of anything." EMET uses brackets to signal the implied word. LOGOS/PNEUMA incorporate it naturally. Consensus follows LOGOS/PNEUMA structure: "a loan of any sort."

---

## v.10–11 — "pledge" (EMET/LOGOS) vs. "collateral" (PNEUMA)

| Agent | Rendering |
|-------|-----------|
| EMET | "take his pledge" / "bring the pledge out to you" |
| LOGOS | "collect his pledge" / "bring the pledge out to you" |
| PNEUMA | "get the collateral he is offering" / "bring the collateral to you himself" |

**Ruling:** Hebrew *'avoto* = "his pledge/security." EMET/LOGOS: "pledge." PNEUMA: "collateral" throughout this section. The chapter uses "pledge" consistently (also in v.12, 13, 17). "Pledge" is the established rendering in the legal sections of Deuteronomy and should be consistent throughout. Consensus follows EMET/LOGOS: "pledge."

---

## v.12 — "you shall not sleep with his pledge" (EMET) vs. "you shall not sleep in his pledge" (LOGOS) vs. "do not keep it overnight" (PNEUMA)

| Agent | Rendering |
|-------|-----------|
| EMET | "you shall not sleep with his pledge" |
| LOGOS | "you shall not sleep in his pledge" |
| PNEUMA | "do not keep it overnight" |

**Ruling:** Hebrew *lo tishkav be-avoto* = "you shall not sleep in/with his pledge." EMET: "with." LOGOS: "in." The preposition *be-* = "in," referring to sleeping wrapped in the cloak being pledged. LOGOS is more precise. PNEUMA's paraphrase ("do not keep it overnight") loses the vivid image of the lender sleeping in the poor man's cloak. Consensus follows LOGOS: "you shall not sleep in his pledge."

---

## v.13 — "certainly return" (EMET) vs. "restore" (LOGOS) vs. "return" (PNEUMA)

| Agent | Rendering |
|-------|-----------|
| EMET | "you shall certainly return the pledge to him" |
| LOGOS | "You shall restore to him the pledge" |
| PNEUMA | "Return his cloak to him by sunset" |

**Ruling:** Hebrew *hashev tashiv* = cognate construction ("return you shall return" = emphatic). EMET: "certainly return" (rendering the cognate intensifier). LOGOS: "restore" (single verb, loses the emphatic). PNEUMA: "return" (single verb, loses the emphatic) and substitutes "his cloak" for "the pledge." Consensus follows EMET: "you shall certainly return the pledge to him."

---

## v.13 — "bless you" (EMET/LOGOS) vs. "thank you" (PNEUMA)

| Agent | Rendering |
|-------|-----------|
| EMET | "that he may sleep in his garment and bless you" |
| LOGOS | "that he may sleep in his cloak and bless you" |
| PNEUMA | "Then he will thank you" |

**Ruling:** Hebrew *uveirkekha* = "and he will bless you." The verb *barak* = "bless," not merely "thank." PNEUMA's "thank you" reduces a covenantal blessing to a social courtesy. Consensus follows EMET/LOGOS: "bless you."

---

## v.13 — "garment" (EMET) vs. "cloak" (LOGOS/PNEUMA)

| Agent | Rendering |
|-------|-----------|
| EMET | "his garment" |
| LOGOS | "his cloak" |
| PNEUMA | "it" (referring back to "cloak" from v.12) |

**Ruling:** Hebrew *simlato* = "his garment/outer cloak." The word refers specifically to the outer garment/cloak. LOGOS: "cloak" is more specific and accurate than "garment." Consensus follows LOGOS: "cloak."

---

## v.13 — "righteousness [tsedaqah]" (EMET) vs. "righteousness" (LOGOS) vs. "a righteous act" (PNEUMA)

| Agent | Rendering |
|-------|-----------|
| EMET | "it shall be righteousness [tsedaqah] to you before the LORD" |
| LOGOS | "it shall be righteousness for you before the LORD your God" |
| PNEUMA | "it will count as a righteous act before the LORD your God" |

**Ruling:** Hebrew *uledkha tihyeh tsedaqah* = "and it shall be righteousness to you." EMET brackets the Hebrew. LOGOS renders cleanly. PNEUMA: "count as a righteous act" introduces the accounting metaphor not present in MT. Consensus follows LOGOS: "it shall be righteousness for you before the LORD your God."

---

## v.14 — "oppress" (EMET/LOGOS) vs. "take advantage of" (PNEUMA)

| Agent | Rendering |
|-------|-----------|
| EMET | "You shall not oppress a hired servant who is poor" |
| LOGOS | "You shall not oppress a hired worker who is poor" |
| PNEUMA | "Do not take advantage of a hired worker who is poor" |

**Ruling:** Hebrew *lo ta'ashok* = "you shall not oppress/extort." EMET/LOGOS: "oppress." PNEUMA: "take advantage of." The verb *'ashaq* carries the force of exploitation under power, not merely unfair dealing — "oppress" is more accurate. Consensus follows EMET/LOGOS: "oppress."

---

## v.14 — "hired servant" (EMET) vs. "hired worker" (LOGOS/PNEUMA)

| Agent | Rendering |
|-------|-----------|
| EMET | "hired servant" |
| LOGOS | "hired worker" |
| PNEUMA | "hired worker" |

**Ruling:** Hebrew *sakir* = "hired man/day laborer." LOGOS/PNEUMA: "hired worker" is the more neutral and accurate modern English term. "Servant" implies a more subordinate or domestic role than the day-laborer context warrants. Consensus follows LOGOS/PNEUMA: "hired worker."

---

## v.15 — "toward it he lifts his soul" (EMET) vs. "counts on it" (LOGOS) vs. "are counting on it" (PNEUMA)

| Agent | Rendering |
|-------|-----------|
| EMET | "toward it he lifts his soul" |
| LOGOS | "he is poor and counts on it" |
| PNEUMA | "they are poor and are counting on it" |

**Ruling:** Hebrew *ve-elav hu nasa' et-nafsho* = "and to it he lifts up his soul." EMET renders literally. LOGOS/PNEUMA: "counts on it" — idiomatic. EMET's rendering is the more vivid and faithful image; the "lifting of the soul" idiom conveys existential longing/dependence. Consensus follows EMET: "toward it he lifts his soul" — preserving the Hebrew idiom, with a note that this is the project's consistent practice for *nefesh* idioms.

---

## v.15 — "it be sin in you" (EMET) vs. "you be guilty of sin" (LOGOS) vs. "you will be guilty of sin" (PNEUMA)

| Agent | Rendering |
|-------|-----------|
| EMET | "lest he cry against you to the LORD, and it be sin in you" |
| LOGOS | "lest he cry against you to the LORD, and you be guilty of sin" |
| PNEUMA | "Otherwise they may cry out to the LORD against you, and you will be guilty of sin" |

**Ruling:** Hebrew *vehayah bekha chet'* = "and there will be in you sin." EMET: "it be sin in you" (literal). LOGOS: "you be guilty of sin." PNEUMA switches to third-person plural ("they") unnecessarily given MT's singular. Consensus follows LOGOS: "you be guilty of sin" — more natural English while preserving the legal weight.

---

## v.16 — "Fathers" (EMET/LOGOS) vs. "Parents" (PNEUMA)

| Agent | Rendering |
|-------|-----------|
| EMET | "Fathers shall not be put to death on account of sons" |
| LOGOS | "Fathers shall not be put to death for their children" |
| PNEUMA | "Parents are not to be put to death for their children's sins" |

**Ruling:** Hebrew *avot lo yamuthu 'al banim* = "fathers shall not be put to death on account of sons." The MT uses *avot* ("fathers") and *banim* ("sons"). PNEUMA uses gender-neutral "parents/children." The Hebrew terms are gender-specific; the legal text concerns patrilineal accountability. Consensus follows EMET/LOGOS: "Fathers shall not be put to death."

---

## v.16 — "on account of sons" (EMET) vs. "for their children" (LOGOS) vs. "for their children's sins" (PNEUMA)

| Agent | Rendering |
|-------|-----------|
| EMET | "on account of sons" / "on account of fathers" |
| LOGOS | "for their children" / "for their fathers" |
| PNEUMA | "for their children's sins" / "for their parents' sins" |

**Ruling:** Hebrew *'al banim* = "on account of / for sons." EMET: "on account of" (most literal). LOGOS: "for." PNEUMA adds "sins" (not in MT for this phrase). Consensus follows LOGOS: "for their children" / "for their fathers."

---

## v.16 — "each man" (EMET) vs. "each one" (LOGOS) vs. "each person" (PNEUMA)

| Agent | Rendering |
|-------|-----------|
| EMET | "each man shall be put to death for his own sin" |
| LOGOS | "Each one shall be put to death for his own sin" |
| PNEUMA | "Each person is to die for their own sin" |

**Ruling:** Hebrew *ish bechet'o yumat* = "a man in his sin shall be put to death." The term *ish* = "man/individual." EMET: "each man." LOGOS: "Each one." PNEUMA: "Each person... their own" (plural pronoun for a singular subject). The Hebrew *ish* is masculine singular; "each man" (EMET) or "each one" (LOGOS) are both accurate. Consensus follows LOGOS: "Each one shall be put to death for his own sin."

---

## v.17 — "pervert the justice due to" (EMET/LOGOS) vs. "deprive... of justice" (PNEUMA)

| Agent | Rendering |
|-------|-----------|
| EMET | "You shall not pervert the justice due to the sojourner or to the orphan" |
| LOGOS | "You shall not pervert the justice due to the sojourner or to the fatherless" |
| PNEUMA | "Do not deprive the sojourner or the orphan of justice" |

**Ruling:** Hebrew *lo tateh mishpat ger yatom* = "you shall not bend/pervert the judgment/justice of the sojourner, the orphan." EMET/LOGOS: "pervert the justice due to." PNEUMA: "deprive... of justice." The verb *natah* = "to bend/pervert/turn aside." "Pervert justice" is the more accurate and weightier rendering. Consensus follows LOGOS.

---

## v.17 — "orphan" (EMET/PNEUMA) vs. "fatherless" (LOGOS)

| Agent | Rendering |
|-------|-----------|
| EMET | "the orphan" |
| LOGOS | "the fatherless" |
| PNEUMA | "the orphan" |

**Ruling:** Hebrew *yatom* = "fatherless child/orphan." Both "orphan" and "fatherless" are legitimate renderings. "Fatherless" is more literal (the Hebrew term does not require the death of both parents). However, "orphan" is the standard translation convention used throughout this project. Consensus follows EMET/PNEUMA: "orphan."

---

## v.19 — "forget a sheaf" (EMET/LOGOS) vs. "overlook a sheaf" (PNEUMA)

| Agent | Rendering |
|-------|-----------|
| EMET | "forget a sheaf in the field" |
| LOGOS | "forget a sheaf in the field" |
| PNEUMA | "you overlook a sheaf" |

**Ruling:** Hebrew *veshakhachta omer* = "and you forget a sheaf." The verb *shakach* = "to forget." PNEUMA: "overlook" softens the term and implies intentional sight rather than genuine forgetting. Consensus follows EMET/LOGOS: "forget a sheaf."

---

## v.20 — "go over the boughs again" (EMET) vs. "go over them again" (LOGOS) vs. "go over the branches a second time" (PNEUMA)

| Agent | Rendering |
|-------|-----------|
| EMET | "you shall not go over the boughs again" |
| LOGOS | "you shall not go over them again" |
| PNEUMA | "do not go over the branches a second time" |

**Ruling:** Hebrew *lo tefa'er acharekha* = "you shall not go over the boughs/gleaning after you." The verb *pa'ar* refers specifically to the post-harvest gleaning pass over the tree. EMET: "boughs" preserves the physical image. LOGOS: "them" (pronoun). PNEUMA: "branches a second time." Consensus follows EMET: "go over the boughs again" — the physical image is instructive.

---

## v.21 — "glean after yourself" (EMET) vs. "strip it afterward" (LOGOS) vs. "go over the vines again" (PNEUMA)

| Agent | Rendering |
|-------|-----------|
| EMET | "you shall not glean after yourself" |
| LOGOS | "you shall not strip it afterward" |
| PNEUMA | "do not go over the vines again" |

**Ruling:** Hebrew *lo te'olel acharekha* = "you shall not glean after you." The verb *'alal* = "to glean/go over again." EMET: "glean after yourself" is the most literal. LOGOS: "strip it afterward." PNEUMA: "go over the vines again." Consensus follows EMET: "glean after yourself" — the gleaning vocabulary links this verse to its context in the gleaning law corpus.

---

## v.22 — "therefore I am commanding you" (EMET) vs. "therefore I command you" (LOGOS/PNEUMA)

| Agent | Rendering |
|-------|-----------|
| EMET | "therefore I am commanding you to do this thing" |
| LOGOS | "therefore I command you to do this thing" |
| PNEUMA | "That is why I am commanding you to do this" |

**Ruling:** Hebrew *'al ken anokhi metsavekha* = "therefore I am commanding you." EMET and PNEUMA use the present continuous "am commanding." LOGOS uses the simple present "command." The Hebrew *metsavekha* is a Piel participle, expressing ongoing command. The present continuous is more accurate. Consensus follows EMET: "therefore I am commanding you to do this thing."

---

*SOPHIA — Deuteronomy 24 disagreements logged: 34*
